lead: Family ties run through today’s two main readings. Abram gathers his household and goes to rescue Lot, the nephew who chose the better land for himself and has been carried off as a prisoner. In John, Jesus’ own “brothers” do not believe in him and urge him to show himself at the festival. Between them, Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal and reads the whole law to the people, and Paul asks, “has God rejected his people?”, and answers, “By no means!” God does not give up on those who are his, and neither does Abram.

set: Genesis 14 is unlike the chapters around it. It reads like an old war record: four kings from the east against five kings of the cities of the Plain. The rulers named have not been securely identified in other ancient sources, and scholars differ about the date of the chapter. Lot, who “settled among the cities of the Plain” (13:12), now lives in Sodom (14:12), and so he is caught up in its defeat.
The reading stops just before the best-known part of the chapter, when Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, brings out bread and wine and blesses Abram (14:18–20).
str: vv. 8–10: the battle in the Valley of Siddim, and the flight.
vv. 11–12: Sodom is plundered, and Lot is taken.
v. 13: the news comes to “Abram the Hebrew”.
vv. 14–16: the pursuit by night, the victory, and everyone is brought back.
kw: This is the first use of the word in the Bible (14:13). Its origin is uncertain. In this story it marks Abram as an outsider in the land.
A word found only here in the Hebrew Bible. These are not a royal army but servants born in his household.

In vv. 14 and 16 the Hebrew calls Lot Abram’s “brother”, although v. 12 has told us that he is his brother’s son. The NRSV rightly says “nephew”. The POC has “brother” in v. 14 and “kinsman” in v. 16. See the question below.
vv: they also took Lot, the son of Abram’s brother, who lived in Sodom,
The narrator reminds us of the family bond and of the place. Lot’s choice in the last chapter has brought him to this.
When Abram heard that his nephew had been taken captive, he led forth his trained men, born in his house,

Abram does not say that Lot deserves what has happened. He gave up the better land without a quarrel, and now he risks his life for the man who took it. The Epistle of Barnabas (9) saw a sign of Jesus and the Cross in the number of these men, 318, written in Greek letters (in substance); this is the kind of symbolic reading some early writers loved, and not the plain sense of the text.
and also brought back his nephew Lot with his goods,
Everything comes back, “the women and the people” as well. Abram takes nothing for himself, as he will tell the king of Sodom (14:22–23).
ch: The next verses of the chapter give the Church one of her oldest images of the Eucharist. The Catechism names Melchizedek as a figure of Christ’s priesthood (CCC 58), and sees in his offering of bread and wine a prefiguring of the Church’s own offering (CCC 1333; see also 1544). So the road of Abram’s rescue ends at a meal of bread and wine, which is a good thought for those who keep the Great Fast on the way to the Holy Qurbana of Easter.

r.h: My time has not yet come
set: The Festival of Booths (Hebrew Sukkot; Leviticus 23:33–43) was a joyful autumn pilgrimage. For seven days the people lived in shelters of branches, remembering the desert, and an eighth day closed the feast. Chapters 7–8 of John take place at this festival.

In v. 1 and v. 13 John’s “the Jews” cannot mean the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his brothers and the crowd are all Jews, and people go in fear of “the Jews” (v. 13). John means the authorities in Jerusalem who were hostile to him (see CCC 597).
str: vv. 1–2: Galilee, the danger in Judea, the festival near.
vv. 3–5: his brothers’ advice: “show yourself to the world”.
vv. 6–9: his reply: “My time has not yet come”.
vv. 10–13: he goes up in secret; the crowds are divided and afraid.
kw: Literally “the setting up of tents”. This is its only use in the New Testament.
The right moment. In vv. 6 and 8 Jesus uses this word, which elsewhere in John gives way to “hour” (hōra). The Malayalam POC has one word, samayam, for both.
A low muttering. It recalls the murmuring of Israel in the desert, the same setting that the festival remembers. Here the POC speaks of people saying many things in secret.
vv: (For not even his brothers believed in him.)
A sad note from the evangelist. Living close to Jesus does not by itself bring faith. On the word “brothers”, see the question below.
My time has not yet come,
His brothers are thinking of publicity, but Jesus lives by the Father’s timetable. “Your time is always here” means that they have nothing they must wait for from God.
Yet no one would speak openly about him for fear of the Jews.

The people are afraid of their leaders, not of their own people. On v. 8, “I am not going to this festival”, many ancient manuscripts have “not yet going”. The NRSV and the POC follow the shorter text. Either way, Jesus refuses to go at his brothers’ urging and for their purpose, and goes later at the Father’s time, “not publicly” (v. 10).
ch: St John’s Gospel keeps asking when and how Jesus will be shown to the world. The Catechism teaches that his “hour” comes at the Passion, when he gives the Spirit (CCC 729–730). For all the opposition reported here, the Church reads these chapters with care: there were believers and doubters among the leaders and among the people, and there was long-standing dispute about him (CCC 595–597).

qa: If Jesus had “brothers”, how can Mary be ever-virgin?

Hebrew and Aramaic have no separate common word for “cousin” or “kinsman”, and “brother” covers them. Today’s first reading is the clearest example: Lot is Abram’s nephew, and the Hebrew calls him his “brother” (14:14, 16). The Catechism cites this very passage when it explains that those called the brothers of Jesus are close relations (CCC 500, citing Genesis 13:8; 14:16). St Jerome made the same argument against Helvidius (in substance).
study: Is there a “Lot” in my family, someone who chose badly and needs my help, not my judgement?
What do I do when God’s timing is not the time I would like?
